questions.stem: Relative scarcity exists because:
options: people's needs and wants are unlimited, while the resources to satisfy them are limited
some goods are produced in quantities too small for every household in the economy to buy one
the prices of most goods and services rise faster than household incomes over time
governments restrict the land, labour and capital that firms are allowed to use
questions.explanation: Relative scarcity is the gap between unlimited needs and wants and the limited resources available to satisfy them. It applies to every good and every economy, whatever the level of prices or incomes, so it is not about prices outpacing incomes.

questions.stem: Mia gives up a four-hour paid shift at a café to attend a free revision lecture. The opportunity cost of attending the lecture is:
options: the value of every other activity she could have done in those four hours
the knowledge and exam marks she expects to gain from the lecture
the wages and other benefits of the shift, her next best alternative
zero, because the lecture itself is free of charge to attend
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, which here is the paid shift. A free lecture still has an opportunity cost, and the cost is only the single best alternative, not the sum of every possible alternative.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the three basic economic questions that every economy must answer?
options: How much should the government borrow each year?
Which industries should receive tariff protection?
How should goods and services be produced?
How should the central bank set interest rates?
questions.explanation: The three basic economic questions are what and how much to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce. Interest rates, borrowing and tariffs are policy decisions some economies make, not the basic questions that arise from relative scarcity.

questions.stem: An economy is producing at a point inside its production possibility frontier. This indicates that:
options: the output combination shown is unattainable with the economy's current resources and technology
some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently, so it is not productively efficient
the economy is producing the combination of goods that society values most highly
the economy has reached the full limit of its current productive capacity
questions.explanation: Points inside the PPF mean more of one good could be produced without giving up any of the other, so resources are idle or wasted. Points on the frontier show full use of capacity, and points beyond it are unattainable.

questions.stem: Which of these changes is most likely to move Australia's whole PPF further from the origin?
options: A fall in unemployment from a recession level
A shift in consumer preferences towards services
A rise in the general level of prices
A rise in the size and skills of the labour force
questions.explanation: The PPF shifts outward when the quantity or quality of resources increases, or technology improves. A fall in unemployment from a recession level moves the economy from inside the frontier towards it, without shifting the frontier itself.

questions.stem: An economy can produce either 100 tonnes of wheat or 50 machines, or any combination along a straight-line PPF between them. The opportunity cost of producing one more machine is:
options: 100 tonnes of wheat
2 tonnes of wheat
0.5 tonnes of wheat
50 tonnes of wheat
questions.explanation: Giving up all 100 tonnes of wheat yields 50 machines, so each machine costs 100 ÷ 50 = 2 tonnes of wheat. The figure of 0.5 tonnes is the opportunity cost the other way round: the machines given up for each tonne of wheat.

questions.stem: A production possibility frontier is usually drawn bowed outward (concave to the origin) because:
options: technology improves automatically as the economy produces more of any one good
firms gain economies of scale as they specialise in producing a single good
resources are not equally suited to every good, so opportunity cost rises as output of one good expands
consumers value each extra unit of a good less than the unit they bought before it, so demand falls as output rises
questions.explanation: As production shifts towards one good, resources less suited to it are drawn in, so each extra unit costs more of the other good. Economies of scale would lower costs as output grew, which is the opposite of a bowed-out frontier.

questions.stem: Allocative efficiency is achieved when:
options: resources are allocated to producing the goods and services that society values most
goods and services are produced at the lowest possible cost per unit of output across the economy
resources move quickly to new uses when consumer preferences or conditions change
resource use is balanced between the needs of present and future generations
questions.explanation: Allocative efficiency is about producing the mix of goods and services that best matches what society wants, maximising living standards. Producing at least cost is productive efficiency, speed of reallocation is dynamic efficiency, and balancing present and future use is intertemporal efficiency.

questions.stem: Productive (technical) efficiency is achieved when:
options: the mix of goods and services produced matches the preferences of consumers as closely as possible
the economy adjusts rapidly to changes in technology and consumer demand over time
the economy saves enough of its resources to meet the needs of future generations
goods are produced at the lowest possible cost, getting the maximum output from given inputs
questions.explanation: Productive efficiency means no resources are wasted: output is produced at minimum cost and the economy operates on its PPF. Matching output to preferences is allocative efficiency, which is a separate condition.

questions.stem: Dynamic efficiency refers to:
options: allocating resources to the goods and services that consumers value most highly today
balancing the use of resources for consumption today against consumption in the future
how quickly and effectively resources are reallocated as preferences and production conditions change
producing each good and service at the lowest possible average cost using the best technology available
questions.explanation: Dynamic efficiency is about the speed and effectiveness with which resources move between uses as conditions change, and it includes the adoption of innovations over time. Least-cost production at a point in time is productive efficiency.

questions.stem: A government requires that a native forest be logged no faster than it regrows, so that it can supply timber for decades to come. This policy is chiefly aimed at improving:
options: intertemporal efficiency
productive efficiency
allocative efficiency
dynamic efficiency
questions.explanation: Intertemporal efficiency concerns the balance between using resources now and conserving them for the future. Limiting the logging rate to the rate of regrowth protects future supply, which is a sustainability goal rather than a cost or preference goal.

questions.stem: A factory reorganises its production line so that the same output is now made with fewer machine hours and less wasted material. This is best described as an improvement in:
options: dynamic efficiency
productive efficiency
allocative efficiency
intertemporal efficiency
questions.explanation: Making the same output with fewer inputs lowers the cost of production, which is productive efficiency. The mix of goods produced has not changed, so allocative efficiency is not the focus.

questions.stem: When demand for home-delivered meals surged, restaurants quickly redeployed kitchen staff and vehicles to delivery, and new delivery platforms entered the market. This speed of adjustment best illustrates:
options: productive efficiency, as each meal was then made at the lowest possible cost
a failure of the price mechanism to signal the change in consumer demand
dynamic efficiency, as resources moved quickly to meet changed preferences
intertemporal efficiency, as resources were conserved for use in later years
questions.explanation: Dynamic efficiency is the ability to reallocate resources quickly as preferences change, and the stem stresses the speed of that adjustment. Nothing in the scenario concerns the cost of each meal or conserving resources for the future.

questions.stem: On a production possibility frontier diagram, allocative efficiency is best shown by:
options: the particular point on the frontier that best matches society's preferences
any point on the frontier, since every such point uses all resources fully
an outward shift of the whole frontier as technology improves over time
a point inside the frontier where some resources are deliberately kept for future use
questions.explanation: Every point on the PPF is productively efficient, but only the combination society values most is allocatively efficient. An outward shift reflects growth in productive capacity, which relates to dynamic and intertemporal efficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a condition of a free and perfectly competitive market?
options: Buyers and sellers have perfect knowledge of prices and products
Each firm sells a slightly different, heavily branded product
A small number of large firms supply most of the market's output
The government sets a minimum price to protect existing producers
questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive market has many buyers and sellers, identical products, perfect knowledge, free entry and exit, and no government interference. Branded products and a few dominant firms describe less competitive market structures.

questions.stem: In a perfectly competitive market, each firm is a price taker because:
options: each firm is too small relative to the market to influence the price
the government regulates the prices charged in competitive industries
firms agree to charge the same price to avoid price wars
consumers are unaware of the prices that rival firms are charging for the same product
questions.explanation: With many firms selling identical products, any one firm that raised its price would lose all its customers to rivals, so it must accept the market price. Consumers in perfect competition have perfect knowledge, so lack of price information cannot be the reason.

questions.stem: Freedom of entry and exit matters in a perfectly competitive market because it:
options: ensures that the government can control the number of firms allowed to operate in the market
lets new firms enter where profits are high, competing those profits away
guarantees that every firm earns a large profit in the long run
allows existing firms to restrict output and raise their prices
questions.explanation: When profits are high, new firms enter, supply rises and price falls until only normal returns remain. Free entry therefore stops firms restricting output to keep prices high, rather than guaranteeing large profits.

questions.stem: According to the law of demand, other things being equal:
options: as income rises, the quantity demanded of every good rises
as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls
as the demand for a good rises, its price falls
as the price of a good rises, demand shifts to the left
questions.explanation: The law of demand describes the inverse relationship between a good's own price and the quantity demanded, shown as a movement along the demand curve. A change in the good's own price never shifts its demand curve.

questions.stem: When the price of a product falls, consumers can buy more of it with the same money income. This part of their response to the price change is called:
options: the profit motive
the income effect
the substitution effect
an increase in demand
questions.explanation: The income effect is the rise in real purchasing power when a good's price falls, which lets consumers buy more. The substitution effect is the switch towards a good because it has become cheaper relative to alternatives.

questions.stem: Bus fares rise while train fares stay the same, and some commuters switch from buses to trains. This is an example of:
options: a leftward shift of the demand curve for bus travel
the substitution effect
the income effect
a decrease in the supply of bus services
questions.explanation: Buses have become dearer relative to trains, so commuters substitute towards the relatively cheaper option. Because the change is in the price of bus travel itself, it is a movement along the demand curve for bus travel, not a shift of it.

questions.stem: A fall in the price of avocados, with no other change in the market, causes:
options: the demand curve for avocados to shift to the right
the supply curve for avocados to shift to the right
a movement up along the demand curve to a lower quantity demanded
a movement down along the demand curve to a higher quantity demanded
questions.explanation: A change in a good's own price causes a movement along its demand curve; a lower price means a larger quantity demanded. Only non-price factors, such as incomes or the prices of related goods, shift the demand curve.

questions.stem: Train fares rise sharply. The demand curve for bus travel on the same routes is most likely to:
options: stay where it is, with a movement down along the curve
shift to the left, as bus travel is a complement to train travel
shift to the right, as bus travel is a substitute for train travel
shift to the left, as bus travel is a substitute for train travel
questions.explanation: Buses and trains on the same routes are substitutes, so dearer train fares make the bus relatively more attractive and increase demand for bus travel at every fare. Bus fares themselves have not changed, so this is a shift rather than a movement along the curve.

questions.stem: The price of petrol rises substantially. What is the most likely effect on the market for large four-wheel-drive vehicles?
options: Demand rises, shifting the demand curve to the right
Demand falls, shifting the demand curve to the left
Supply falls, shifting the supply curve to the left
Quantity demanded falls along an unchanged demand curve
questions.explanation: Petrol and fuel-hungry vehicles are complements, so a rise in the price of petrol reduces demand for large four-wheel drives at every price. The vehicles' own price has not changed, so it is a shift of demand rather than a movement along it.

questions.stem: A rise in interest rates is most likely to shift the demand curve for new houses:
options: nowhere, because only a change in house prices can affect demand for houses
to the left, because loan repayments rise and borrowing becomes less attractive
to the right, because households with savings now earn more interest income each year
to the left, because house prices themselves have risen with interest rates
questions.explanation: Most home purchases are financed by borrowing, so higher interest rates raise repayments and reduce demand at every price. A change in the price of houses causes a movement along the curve, and non-price factors such as interest rates do shift demand.

questions.stem: An ageing population is most likely to increase demand for:
options: university places for school leavers
first-home loans for young buyers
aged-care and health services
childcare places for young children
questions.explanation: Population demographics are a non-price factor affecting demand. A larger share of older people increases demand for goods and services they use most, such as aged care and health services.

questions.stem: A cut in income tax rates raises households' disposable incomes. What is the most likely effect on the market for restaurant meals?
options: Demand shifts right, raising price but lowering quantity traded
Quantity demanded rises along a fixed demand curve, lowering price
Demand shifts right, raising equilibrium price and quantity traded
Supply shifts right, lowering price and raising quantity traded
questions.explanation: Higher disposable income increases demand for normal goods such as restaurant meals, shifting demand to the right. With supply unchanged, both the equilibrium price and the quantity traded rise.

questions.stem: Consumer confidence falls sharply as households worry about job security. The demand curve for new cars is most likely to:
options: stay in place, as confidence only affects the supply of cars
shift to the left, as car makers cut production in response
shift to the left, as households postpone large purchases
shift to the right, as households buy cars before prices rise
questions.explanation: Consumer confidence is a non-price factor affecting demand, and lower confidence leads households to delay big purchases such as cars. Car makers cutting production would be a change in supply, not demand.

questions.stem: According to the law of supply, a higher price leads to a larger quantity supplied because:
options: the costs of producing each extra unit fall as the market price of the good rises
consumers are willing to buy more of a good when its price is higher
governments lower the taxes on a good whenever its market price rises
of the profit motive: a higher price makes producing more units more profitable
questions.explanation: The law of supply rests on the profit motive: a higher price makes extra output profitable, so producers offer more. Consumers buy less, not more, at higher prices, which is the law of demand.

questions.stem: Wages in the construction industry rise sharply. In the market for new apartments, the supply curve will:
options: shift to the left, lowering price and reducing the quantity traded
shift to the left, raising price and reducing the quantity traded
shift to the right, raising price and increasing the quantity traded
stay in place while the demand curve for apartments shifts left
questions.explanation: Wages are a cost of production, so higher wages reduce supply at every price and shift the supply curve left. With demand unchanged, the equilibrium price rises and the quantity traded falls.

questions.stem: A severe frost damages much of Victoria's stone fruit crop. In the local market for peaches, the most likely outcome is that:
options: supply decreases, so the equilibrium price falls and the quantity traded rises
quantity supplied falls along an unchanged supply curve, and price is steady
supply decreases, so the equilibrium price rises and the quantity traded falls
demand decreases, so the equilibrium price falls and the quantity traded falls
questions.explanation: Climatic conditions are a non-price factor affecting supply, and a frost reduces the quantity growers can offer at every price. A leftward shift of supply raises the equilibrium price and lowers the quantity traded.

questions.stem: Which of the following would shift the supply curve for wheat to the right?
options: Several large growers leaving the industry
Higher-yielding seed varieties that raise output per hectare
A rise in the market price of wheat
An increase in the wages paid to farm workers
questions.explanation: Improved technology and productivity lower costs per unit and increase supply at every price. A rise in the price of wheat moves producers along the supply curve rather than shifting it.

questions.stem: Many new cafés open in a suburb at the same time as a large office complex nearby closes. The most likely effect on the local market for coffee is:
options: a fall in both the price and the quantity traded
a fall in price, with the change in quantity traded uncertain
a rise in price, with the change in quantity traded uncertain
a fall in quantity traded, with the change in price uncertain
questions.explanation: More suppliers shift supply right and the loss of office workers shifts demand left; both changes push price down. Their effects on quantity work in opposite directions, so the change in quantity traded depends on the relative sizes of the shifts.

questions.stem: If the price of a product is above its equilibrium level, then:
options: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so buyers bid the price higher until the market clears
the demand curve shifts to the right until the market clears
the supply curve shifts to the left until the market clears
quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, putting downward pressure on price
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, producers offer more than consumers want to buy, creating a surplus. Sellers cut prices to clear stock, moving the market back down the curves to equilibrium; neither curve needs to shift.

questions.stem: Demand and supply for electric bicycles both increase, and the increase in demand is larger than the increase in supply. The equilibrium:
options: price falls and quantity traded rises
price rises and quantity traded falls
price is unchanged and quantity traded rises
price rises and quantity traded rises
questions.explanation: Both a rise in demand and a rise in supply increase the quantity traded. Their effects on price work in opposite directions, but because the demand increase is larger, the upward pressure on price wins.

questions.stem: In a market, 600 units are demanded and 300 supplied at $4; 450 are demanded and 450 supplied at $6; and 300 are demanded and 600 supplied at $8. At a price of $4 the market has:
options: a shortage of 150 units, so the price will tend to rise towards $8
a surplus of 150 units, so the price will tend to rise towards $6
a shortage of 300 units, so the price will tend to rise towards $6
a surplus of 300 units, so the price will tend to fall below $4
questions.explanation: At $4, quantity demanded (600) exceeds quantity supplied (300) by 300 units, which is a shortage. Buyers compete for the limited stock and the price rises to $6, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

questions.stem: Price elasticity of demand measures:
options: the responsiveness of the quantity supplied by producers to a change in the good's own price
the responsiveness of the quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price
the responsiveness of demand for a good to a change in consumers' incomes
how far a good's price changes when its demand curve shifts to the right
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Responsiveness to income is a different measure, and responsiveness of quantity supplied is price elasticity of supply.

questions.stem: A streaming service raises its monthly price by 10 per cent and its number of subscribers falls by 25 per cent. Demand for the service is:
options: price inelastic, with a coefficient of 2.5, so total revenue falls
price elastic, with a coefficient of 2.5, so total revenue falls
price inelastic, with a coefficient of 0.4, so total revenue rises
price elastic, with a coefficient of 2.5, so total revenue rises
questions.explanation: The coefficient is 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5, which is greater than 1, so demand is price elastic. When demand is elastic, a price rise causes a proportionally larger fall in quantity, so total revenue falls.

questions.stem: A firm lowers its price from $20 to $16 and its weekly sales rise from 1000 to 1100 units. Which statement is correct?
options: Demand is price elastic, and total revenue rises by $2400
Demand is price inelastic, and total revenue falls by $2400
Demand is price elastic, and total revenue falls by $2400
Demand is price inelastic, and total revenue rises by $1600
questions.explanation: Price falls by 20 per cent and quantity rises by 10 per cent, a coefficient of 0.5, so demand is inelastic. Revenue falls from $20 000 to $17 600, a drop of $2400, as expected when price is cut and demand is inelastic.

questions.stem: Demand for insulin among people who need it is highly price inelastic mainly because:
options: consumers have plenty of time to adjust their purchases
it is a luxury good bought mainly by high-income earners
it is a necessity with no close substitutes
it takes up a large proportion of most incomes
questions.explanation: Goods that are necessities and have no close substitutes have inelastic demand, because buyers keep purchasing them when price rises. A large share of income and a long time to adjust would both make demand more elastic, not less.

questions.stem: Demand for new cars is more price elastic than demand for table salt, mainly because:
options: cars are considered a necessity by most Australian households
the price of table salt changes more often than the price of cars
a car takes up a much larger proportion of a household's income
table salt has a wider range of close substitutes than cars
questions.explanation: When a good takes a large share of income, a price change has a big effect on the budget, so buyers respond more. Salt costs so little that a price change barely matters; and being a necessity would make car demand less elastic, not more.

questions.stem: Demand for petrol tends to become more price elastic over a longer period because:
options: refiners have more time to build new capacity and increase the supply of petrol
petrol becomes more of a necessity as people choose to live further from work
the prices of complements to petrol, such as cars, tend to rise over time
consumers have more time to find substitutes, such as more efficient or electric cars
questions.explanation: Over time consumers can change their behaviour and their vehicles, so the quantity demanded responds more to a price change. Refiners building capacity is a supply response, which affects price elasticity of supply rather than demand.

questions.stem: A manufacturer has idle machines and workers it can call on at short notice. Its supply is likely to be:
options: relatively price elastic, as output can be raised quickly without much extra cost
relatively price inelastic, as it cannot raise output until it builds a new factory
perfectly price inelastic in the short run, whatever happens to the market price
relatively price elastic, because demand for the manufacturer's product is elastic
questions.explanation: Spare capacity lets a producer increase output quickly when price rises, which makes supply price elastic. Elasticity of supply depends on producers' ability to respond, not on the elasticity of demand for the product.

questions.stem: Supply of fresh flowers for the week before Mother's Day is more price inelastic than supply of canned soup. The main reason is that:
options: flower growers usually operate with large amounts of spare capacity in the weeks before
flowers have a long production period and are perishable, while soup is durable and can be stockpiled
flowers are a luxury, so demand for them is more price elastic than demand for canned soup
soup producers face higher costs of production than flower growers do for each unit sold
questions.explanation: Flowers take months to grow and cannot be stored, so growers cannot quickly add to supply when price spikes. Soup is durable, so producers can build stocks in advance and release them, which makes supply more elastic.

questions.stem: The price of wool falls relative to the prices of other farm products. The price mechanism is most likely to:
options: draw more resources into wool growing, as the lower price signals that wool is scarce
raise the quantity of wool supplied, as buyers now want more wool at the lower price
leave the allocation of resources unchanged, as prices only signal to consumers
shift farmland and labour out of wool growing into products that now earn higher returns
questions.explanation: A fall in a good's relative price signals that society values it less and lowers the profit from producing it, so resources move towards goods whose relative prices have risen. Prices signal to producers as well as consumers, which is how the market reallocates resources.

questions.stem: Over a year, the price of beef rises 2 per cent while the general price level rises 6 per cent. Which statement is correct?
options: Beef producers will expand output, because the price of beef has increased
Relative prices are unchanged, because beef and other prices both rose
The relative price of beef has fallen, signalling a smaller reward for producing beef
The relative price of beef has risen, attracting more resources into beef production
questions.explanation: Resources respond to relative prices, not absolute ones. Beef's price rose by less than prices in general, so beef became relatively cheaper and relatively less rewarding to produce, even though its money price went up.
